Consult Summary:
- 27-year-old male with an insect sting to the right arm a few minutes prior, reporting localized rash and subjective breathing difficulty and mild oral/tongue sensation.
- On video exam there is a puncture mark and mild redness on the arm, no visible significant swelling, no signs of airway compromise; managed as a localized allergic reaction with advice to take oral antihistamine and seek urgent care if symptoms worsen.

Problem List:

Issue 1:
- Insect sting (possible bee or wasp) to right arm, onset a few minutes before consult.
- Symptoms: localised redness and puncture mark at sting site; patient reports a rash, mild soreness; subjective feeling of difficulty breathing and "weird" tongue sensation; patient reports possible mild lip swelling.
- Systems review/pertinent negatives: breathing and speech appear normal on video; clinician observed no inspiratory stridor, no visible lip or oropharyngeal swelling, and normal breathing at time of assessment.
- Examination findings: puncture mark on right arm with mild redness/blotchy rash; oral/throat inspection (patient said "ah")—no edema of lips or pharyngeal soft tissues noted.
- Impression/differential: localized allergic/inflammatory reaction to insect sting. Anaphylaxis/airway compromise not evident at time of assessment.
- Management given: advised oral antihistamine (chlorphenamine/Piriton 4 mg — one tablet, up to six times daily); alternative "one-a-day" antihistamine option mentioned (agent/dose not documented). Advised to purchase OTC antihistamine at pharmacy. Advised urgent A&E if any progression of breathing difficulty, lip/throat swelling, stridor, or rapid deterioration. Advised to seek GP/Babylon review if concerned or if redness spreads/feels hot (possible local infection) — antibiotics may be considered if infection suspected. Patient given information link about anaphylaxis.

Issue 2:
- Anxiety / occasional panic attacks.
- History: patient reports occasional anxiety/panic attacks; not on medication for anxiety.
- Relevance: anxiety noted as contributing to perception of breathing difficulty; clinician provided reassurance and lower threshold to contact service if worried.

Issue 3:
- No additional active issues discussed.
- Note: patient uncertain whether insect was a bee or wasp.

Medications:
- None taken for this event at time of consult.
- Chlorphenamine (Piriton) recommended: 4 mg tablet, up to six times daily (per clinician advice).
- "One-a-day" antihistamine option mentioned (agent/dose not documented).

Allergies:
- Penicillin.

Past Medical History:
- Eczema.

Social History:
- Age 27, works as a computer scientist.
- Lives alone.
- Owns a cat.
- Occasional anxiety/panic attacks; not on treatment.

Preventative History:
- No preventative care items (cervical screen, mammogram, PSA, FOBT, bone density, vaccinations, optometry, skin check) were discussed or documented.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: not documented.
- Right arm: puncture mark with mild redness/blotchy rash; no significant swelling observed.
- Mouth/throat: inspected by video with patient phonation ("ah"); clinician observed no oral/pharyngeal soft tissue swelling or airway compromise.
- Respiratory: breathing appears normal on video; no stridor noted.

Plan:
- Immediate: patient to take OTC oral antihistamine (chlorphenamine 4 mg tablet, up to every 4–6 hours as advised; alternative once-daily antihistamine option acceptable).
- Safety-netting: urgent ED/A&E if any signs of airway compromise (increasing difficulty breathing, wheeze, stridor, progressive lip/tongue/throat swelling), or if symptoms progress rapidly.
- If local redness spreads, becomes hot, or shows signs of infection: consider GP review and possible antibiotics.
- Follow-up: contact Babylon/GP if worsening or ongoing symptoms; clinician to provide information link on anaphylaxis for patient education.
- Longer-term: no allergy testing indicated presently; consider referral/testing if recurrent reactions.

Quality checks (always include at bottom of note, or fill document_quality):
- Missing but clinically expected elements: vital signs (respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, heart rate, blood pressure), exact current medications (medication reconciliation), documentation whether epinephrine was available or prescribed, and specific agent/dose for the "one-a-day" antihistamine option.
- Internal conflicts: patient reports subjective lip swelling and altered tongue sensation while clinician observed no lip/oral swelling on exam — conflict noted. Patient uncertain whether insect was a bee or wasp.
- Transcript quality: clear, minimal background noise; clinician and patient responses intelligible.
